story_areas.name: Smart planner

story_areas.name: Attendance

US-001.moment: Priya opens CampusMate on the family laptop, taps "Sign in with Google" and lands on her dashboard. No new password to invent or forget.
US-001.analogy: Like walking into the college library with the ID card you already have, instead of applying for a separate library pass.

US-002.moment: Priya finishes revising on a study-centre computer and taps "Sign out". The next student who sits down sees only the login screen.
US-002.analogy: Like locking your locker before you leave the library.

US-003.moment: Priya changes "Priya S" to "Priya Sharma". After graduating, she deletes her account and every note, plan and mark is gone.
US-003.analogy: Like handing back your hostel room key: you change the name on the door while you live there, and you clear everything out when you leave.

US-004.moment: On her very first visit, CampusMate asks for her five subjects and how many hours she can study each day, so her dashboard isn't an empty page.
US-004.analogy: Like the first page of a new diary, where you write your timetable before anything else.

US-005.moment: Priya adds "DBMS", fixes the typo in "Cumputer Networks", and deletes an elective she dropped, along with its old assignments.
US-005.analogy: Subjects are the folders in your school bag. Every assignment, note and attendance mark goes inside one.

US-006.moment: Priya sets her DBMS exam for 12 December and marks Maths as a weak subject. The dashboard now says "DBMS exam in 9 days".
US-006.analogy: Like circling exam dates in red on the wall calendar and putting a star next to the subject you find hardest.

US-007.moment: Priya enters her counselling sessions: DBMS every Monday and Wednesday, 6 to 7 pm. On Monday the dashboard shows them under "Today's classes".
US-007.analogy: Like the class timetable pinned on the noticeboard. The app needs its own copy to know what "today" looks like.

US-008.moment: Each morning Priya opens one screen: two classes today, a DBMS assignment due tomorrow, Maths exam in 9 days, Networks attendance at risk, and a 5-day streak.
US-008.analogy: Like a car dashboard: fuel, speed and warning lights in one glance, without opening the bonnet.

US-009.moment: Her dashboard says: "Revise normalisation in DBMS for 45 minutes. Your exam is in 9 days." It says the same thing all day, and something new tomorrow.
US-009.analogy: Like a tutor who leaves you one sticky note each morning instead of giving a lecture.

US-010.moment: Priya says she has 2 hours a day. CampusMate builds a plan from today to her last exam, giving Maths extra time.
US-010.analogy: Like a GPS planning the route to your exam date, given how much fuel (time) you have each day.

US-011.moment: Priya set "2 hours a day" once. Next week, when she regenerates her plan, the form already says 2.
US-011.analogy: Like your phone remembering your home address so you don't type it every time you book a cab.

US-012.moment: Priya opens the timetable and sees Monday to Sunday: today highlighted, finished sessions marked done, the one she missed marked missed.
US-012.analogy: The weekly spread in a paper planner.

US-013.moment: After 45 minutes on DBMS, Priya ticks the session done. It turns green and she earns 10 XP.
US-013.analogy: Ticking a box on your to-do list, and getting a gold star for it.

US-014.moment: Her shift ran late and she missed Thursday's Maths session. She marks it missed, and the rest of the week reshuffles to fit it back in.
US-014.analogy: Like GPS recalculating when you miss a turn, instead of telling you to drive back to where you went wrong.

US-015.moment: The DBMS exam moves from 12 to 20 December. Priya taps "Regenerate plan" and her sessions spread out over the extra week.
US-015.analogy: Re-planning a trip when the train date changes.

US-016.moment: The AI is overloaded. Priya sees "The AI service is unavailable, try again later", and her existing plan is untouched.
US-016.analogy: Like an ATM that shows "Out of service" instead of swallowing your card and giving you no cash.

US-017.moment: Priya uploads a 20-page DBMS PDF and gets a one-page summary of the key points a moment later.
US-017.analogy: Like a friend who reads the whole chapter and gives you the key points on one page.

US-018.moment: From the same PDF, CampusMate writes 8 multiple-choice questions about normalisation and keys.
US-018.analogy: Like a friend who quizzes you from your own notes the night before an exam.

US-019.moment: Priya answers the 8 questions, scores 6 out of 8, and sees the correct answer for the two she got wrong.
US-019.analogy: A practice test that is marked the moment you hand it in.

US-020.moment: On the DBMS note, Priya sees her scores go from 4/8 to 6/8 to 8/8 over a week.
US-020.analogy: Like the marks on your report cards across a term, showing you improving.

US-021.moment: Priya types "normal" in the search box and finds "Normalisation notes" among 30 uploads. She deletes an old draft she no longer needs.
US-021.analogy: A library catalogue instead of a pile of photocopies on your desk.

US-022.moment: The summary skipped the topic Priya cared about. She taps "Regenerate summary" and gets a better one; her old quiz scores stay.
US-022.analogy: Asking a friend to explain it again, a different way.

US-023.moment: Priya tries to upload a Word file. CampusMate tells her straight away it accepts PDF and text files only.
US-023.analogy: Like a vending machine that hands back a foreign coin and shows which coins it takes.

US-024.moment: The WhatsApp group announces "DBMS assignment due 30 Nov". Priya adds it to CampusMate in ten seconds.
US-024.analogy: Writing the deadline in your diary instead of trusting the group chat to remind you.

US-025.moment: The deadline is extended to 5 December. Priya edits the date instead of deleting and re-adding the assignment.
US-025.analogy: Correcting the date in your diary, rather than starting a new diary.

US-026.moment: Priya submits her assignment and marks it done: +20 XP. She reopens it by accident and completes it again, and gets no extra XP.
US-026.analogy: Stamping "Submitted" on your assignment. One submission gets one stamp.

US-027.moment: The assignment due tomorrow carries a "Due soon" tag on her dashboard.
US-027.analogy: A yellow highlighter on the urgent line in your diary.

US-028.moment: Priya missed a deadline. That assignment shows "Overdue" until she completes it.
US-028.analogy: The "overdue" stamp on a library book you forgot to return.

US-029.moment: A small bell in the header shows "2". Tapping it lists the two assignments that need her attention.
US-029.analogy: A notice board at the college gate that you see every time you walk in. It won't phone you at home.

US-030.moment: After class Priya marks herself present. Networks shows 17 of 24: 70.8%.
US-030.analogy: The teacher's attendance register, but in your pocket.

US-031.moment: Priya accidentally marked last Monday absent. She opens the history and changes it to present.
US-031.analogy: Rubbing out a pencil mistake in the register.

US-032.moment: DBMS says "You can miss 2 more classes". Networks says "Attend the next 4 classes".
US-032.analogy: Like a phone battery that says "3 hours left" instead of just "62%".

US-033.moment: DBMS is at exactly 75% (18 of 24), but CampusMate shows "At risk", because one more absence would drop it to 72%.
US-033.analogy: The fuel light that comes on before the tank is empty, not after.

US-034.moment: Every finished assignment gives Priya 20 XP and every finished study session 10 XP.
US-034.analogy: Points on a supermarket loyalty card for every purchase.

US-035.moment: Priya has studied 5 days in a row. If she skips a whole day, the count goes back to 0.
US-035.analogy: A daily watering chart for a plant: miss a day and you start counting again.

US-036.moment: On day 7 of her streak, a message pops up: "Badge unlocked: 7-Day Streak".
US-036.analogy: Scout badges sewn onto a sash, one for each milestone.

US-037.moment: With 240 XP Priya is level 3, and the bar shows 40 of 100 XP to level 4.

US-038.moment: Priya's profile shows her XP, level, streak and every badge she has earned, with the dates. Locked badges show what she needs to do.
US-038.analogy: A trophy shelf, with empty spaces labelled for the trophies still to win.

US-039.moment: Sunday evening, Priya opens the weekly report: 6 h 30 min studied, 3 of 4 assignments done.
US-039.analogy: The weekly summary in a fitness app, but for studying.

US-040.moment: Before meeting her guide, Priya opens the attendance report: every subject, classes held, attended, percentage and status.

US-041.moment: The assignment report shows DBMS: 3 completed, 1 overdue; Maths: 2 pending.
US-041.analogy: The teacher's assignment register, sorted by subject.

US-042.moment: Two weeks before exams, Priya opens the notes log and reads every summary in one list.
US-042.analogy: A revision folder of one-page cheat sheets.

US-043.moment: Rahul is also on CampusMate. Even if he guesses the web address of one of Priya's notes, he gets "not found".
US-043.analogy: Your bank shows only your account, even if you type someone else's account number.

US-044.moment: In class, Priya logs attendance from her phone. Every screen fits without scrolling sideways.
US-044.analogy: A pocket diary and a desk diary with the same pages.

ADR-001.plain: CampusMate is split into three layers: the screens students see (Angular), the brain that applies the rules (FastAPI), and the memory that stores everything (the database).
ADR-001.analogy: A restaurant: the dining room (screens), the kitchen (rules), the storeroom (database). Customers never walk into the kitchen, so the secret recipe (the AI key) stays safe.
ADR-001.means: You learn two languages instead of one, and in return the AI key stays safe and the code matches the diagrams in your synopsis.

ADR-002.plain: Screens are built from Angular Material's ready-made buttons, forms and dialogs, then restyled with a bold CampusMate theme and smooth, playful animations so the app feels modern rather than stock.
ADR-002.analogy: Buying a well-built flat-pack wardrobe and then painting it, adding new handles and lights: sturdy inside, your own style outside.
ADR-002.means: You keep Material's accessibility and save weeks of building; the custom look and animations add about 3–4 days in the polish week.

ADR-003.plain: The back end is written in Python using FastAPI, which checks every incoming request automatically before your code runs.
ADR-003.analogy: A guard at the kitchen door who checks every order slip is filled in properly before the cook sees it.
ADR-003.means: The synopsis names FastAPI without a reason; this gives you the answer when the examiner asks.

ADR-004.plain: Students sign in only with their Google account. CampusMate never stores a password.
ADR-004.analogy: Using an ID card students already carry instead of printing your own passes.
ADR-004.means: No password system to build or protect; students without a Google account can't use the app.

ADR-005.plain: All AI features use free models through one service, OpenRouter, called only from the server. Swapping models is a settings change.
ADR-005.analogy: A free shared taxi stand with many drivers: it costs nothing, but some days there are few taxis and you only get a few rides.
ADR-005.means: Zero cost, but daily request limits and changing models are permanent facts of life for the project.

ADR-006.plain: Use the simple file-based SQLite on your laptop, and a free PostgreSQL database when the app is online.
ADR-006.analogy: Practise in a rough notebook at home, but keep the final records in the college office's filing cabinet, because the free host clears its desks every night.
ADR-006.means: Without this, every student's data on the live app could vanish the next time you deploy.

ADR-007.plain: Every record gets a long random id like 3f9c…a1, not 1, 2, 3.
ADR-007.analogy: Random locker codes instead of lockers numbered 1, 2, 3, so nobody can guess the next one.
ADR-007.means: Tiny cost; web addresses can't be guessed to reach other students' data.

ADR-008.plain: A note's AI summary and quiz are stored on the note itself; each quiz attempt is stored separately.
ADR-008.analogy: Stapling the summary sheet to the back of the notes instead of filing it in a different cabinet.
ADR-008.means: Simpler code, but you should explain in the report why the quiz isn't split into question tables.

ADR-009.plain: Store each earned badge as its own row with the date earned, instead of a list squeezed into one column.
ADR-009.analogy: A proper register with one line per badge and date, rather than badge names scribbled in a margin.
ADR-009.means: One more table, and a schema the examiner can't fault for breaking normal form.

ADR-010.plain: When a student misses a session, ask the AI to rebuild the rest of the plan. Finished and missed sessions stay as history; if the AI fails, nothing changes.
ADR-010.analogy: GPS recalculating the route after a missed turn.
ADR-010.means: Plans stay realistic, but every missed session uses one AI request.

ADR-011.plain: One shared check runs on every request to make sure a student only ever touches their own records.
ADR-011.analogy: Every bank teller follows the same rule: check the passbook matches the customer before showing anything.
ADR-011.means: One place to get right; skipping it would let one student read another's notes.

ADR-012.plain: The dashboard's AI suggestion is created once per student per day and saved, not on every page load.
ADR-012.analogy: Writing today's thought on the classroom whiteboard once each morning, instead of every time someone walks in.
ADR-012.means: Protects the free AI quota; the tip can't change during the day.

ADR-013.plain: The 75% rule lives in one setting, and the maths uses whole numbers so 75% is never miscounted.
ADR-013.analogy: A thermostat dial set to 75, instead of a wire soldered at 75.
ADR-013.means: Easy to change for another university; exact results at the boundary.

ADR-014.plain: When a note is uploaded, keep its text in the database and throw the file away in the live app.
ADR-014.analogy: Photocopying the important pages into your register and returning the book, instead of renting a shelf for it.
ADR-014.means: No paid storage needed; students can't re-download the original file from the live app.

ADR-015.plain: Read text from typed PDFs and text files only. Scanned pages and handwriting are refused with a clear message, unless a free AI that can read images becomes available.
ADR-015.analogy: A scanner that reads printed pages perfectly but can't read your handwriting.
ADR-015.means: Reliable from day one, but you must say in the synopsis that handwritten notes aren't supported yet.

ADR-016.plain: Screens are hosted on Firebase Hosting, the back end on Render, and the database on Neon, all on free plans.
ADR-016.analogy: Three free stalls at a college fair: posters at one, the counter at another, the storeroom at a third. The counter staff nap when it's quiet, so the first visitor waits a minute.
ADR-016.means: Free and reachable by your evaluator; open the app a minute before your demo to wake it up.

ADR-017.plain: Talk to the database through SQLAlchemy and record every change to the table structure with Alembic.
ADR-017.analogy: A translator who speaks both SQLite and PostgreSQL, plus a logbook of every change to the building's floor plan.
ADR-017.means: Lets you switch databases safely, and the logbook doubles as proof you did the work.

ADR-018.plain: Every AI call waits at most 60 seconds, tries once more, then tries a backup model, checks the answer, and saves nothing unless it's all good.
ADR-018.analogy: Ordering from a busy kitchen: wait a set time, ask again, try the kitchen next door, and inspect the dish before serving. Never serve half a plate.
ADR-018.means: Predictable errors and no half-saved plans; students may wait on a spinner.

ADR-019.plain: Deadline reminders appear inside the app only: a bell and labels on the dashboard. No emails or phone notifications.
ADR-019.analogy: A notice board at the college gate, not a phone call at home.
ADR-019.means: Nothing extra to host; a student who doesn't open the app gets no reminder.

ADR-020.plain: Every student's "today" is worked out in their own time zone, saved when they first sign in.
ADR-020.analogy: Indian train timetables are printed in IST even if the railway's computers are abroad.
ADR-020.means: Streaks and overdue labels stay correct wherever the server runs.

ADR-021.plain: Each XP award is written once in a ledger with a unique receipt number, so the same assignment can't pay out twice.
ADR-021.analogy: A receipt book where each receipt number can only be used once.
ADR-021.means: Stops XP farming by ticking and unticking; one more table.

ADR-022.plain: Only use AI providers that don't keep or train on what's sent, tell students their notes go to an outside AI, and never send names or emails.
ADR-022.analogy: Taking your notes to an outside print shop: you choose one that promises not to keep copies, and you tell the owner of the notes.
ADR-022.means: Students are informed and safer; fewer free models may qualify.

ADR-023.plain: Deleting a subject deletes everything inside it; deleting an account deletes everything. A confirmation shows exactly what will go.
ADR-023.analogy: Throwing away a folder throws away the pages inside it.
ADR-023.means: No messy leftovers; there is no undo.

ADR-024.plain: Each student can make up to 20 AI requests a day.
ADR-024.analogy: The canteen gives each student 20 coupons a day, so the first in the queue can't take all the food.
ADR-024.means: Fair for everyone; a student cramming for exams may hit the limit.

ADR-025.plain: All server addresses follow one pattern, /api/v1/subjects, /api/v1/notes and so on, and errors always look the same.
ADR-025.analogy: Standard house numbers on a street, so the postman always finds the right door.
ADR-025.means: Cleaner code and tests; changing it later means changing every address.

ADR-026.plain: One GitHub repository with three folders: frontend, backend and docs.
ADR-026.analogy: One project binder with three tabbed sections instead of three separate binders.
ADR-026.means: One history of all your work, which is the evidence of originality the guidelines ask for.

ADR-027.plain: Passwords and keys live in environment settings that never go into GitHub; the repo holds only an example file.
ADR-027.analogy: Keeping your house key in your pocket, not under the doormat of a public building.
ADR-027.means: The repository is public, so this is what keeps your AI key from being stolen.

ADR-028.plain: Automated tests use recorded AI answers instead of the real AI, and run on every push to GitHub.
ADR-028.analogy: Pilots practise in a flight simulator with recorded scenarios instead of real planes.
ADR-028.means: Free, repeatable test evidence for the report; a few live checks are still needed before submission.

ADR-029.plain: Reports are calculated fresh each time they're opened, can be downloaded as CSV, and printed from the browser.
ADR-029.analogy: Your bank calculating your balance when you check, instead of printing yesterday's.
ADR-029.means: Always accurate and simple; no history of past weeks.

ADR-030.plain: The back end has one folder per feature, and each folder splits the work into a route (the web address), a controller (turns problems into clear error messages) and a service (the actual rules and database work).
ADR-030.analogy: A hospital department: reception takes your request (route), a nurse decides where it goes and explains any problem (controller), and the doctor does the actual work (service). Every department is organised the same way.
ADR-030.means: About five small files per feature; in return every bug points to one file and the rules can be tested on their own.

ADR-031.plain: The front end has three areas: core (sign-in and the page frame used everywhere), shared (reusable pieces like spinners and dialogs) and features (one folder per screen group, loaded only when opened).
ADR-031.analogy: A shopping mall: building services (core) serve every shop, benches and lifts (shared) belong to no single shop, and each shop (feature) keeps its own stock and opens only when a customer walks in.
ADR-031.means: More folders and a little setup per feature; in return a faster first load and features that can't break each other.
